projectBackground.name: Alpine Retail Bank AML Uplift
projectBackground.context: A monitoring alert shows repeated deposits just below the reporting threshold, and a new customer is linked to a politically exposed person.

manager.name: Sofia Brun
manager.note: Compliance is judged on what you can evidence. Document why you escalated, why you didn't, and never alert the customer.

assignment.title: Triage the alerts and file the report
assignment.brief: Identify structuring, determine the right due diligence level, compute the aggregate and write a SAR narrative that does not tip off the customer.

documents.name: Transaction Alert
documents.note: Four cash deposits of CHF 9,500 in one week; threshold for reporting is CHF 10,000.

documents.name: Customer Profile
documents.note: New account; director is a close relative of a senior public official.

documents.name: SAR Template
documents.note: Fields: subject, activity, reasons for suspicion, supporting documents.

tasks.title: Recognising Structuring
tasks.prompt: A customer makes several deposits just under the reporting threshold within days. This pattern is known as:
options: Structuring (smurfing), a common money-laundering red flag
tasks.reasoning: Splitting amounts to avoid thresholds is a classic indicator.
tasks.tip: Look at the pattern, not the individual transaction.
tasks.mistake: Reviewing each deposit in isolation misses the pattern.
tasks.recommendation: Write down your reasoning and the evidence behind it so a reviewer can verify your conclusion quickly.

tasks.title: Aggregate Amount
tasks.prompt: Four deposits of CHF 9,500 were made in one week. What is the total deposited?
tasks.reasoning: Aggregating shows the true amount, which exceeds the threshold four times over.
tasks.mistake: Reviewing deposits individually hides the total.
tasks.recommendation: Write down your reasoning and the evidence behind it so a reviewer can verify your conclusion quickly.

tasks.title: Politically Exposed Persons
tasks.prompt: A new customer's director is a close relative of a senior public official. What is the correct approach?
options: Apply enhanced due diligence, including source of wealth and senior management approval
tasks.reasoning: PEP links carry higher corruption risk and require enhanced due diligence, not automatic refusal.
tasks.mistake: Automatic rejection or ignoring both fail the risk-based standard.
tasks.recommendation: Write down your reasoning and the evidence behind it so a reviewer can verify your conclusion quickly.

tasks.title: Red Flags
tasks.prompt: Select the red flags in this case.
options: Customer opened account with valid ID
Regular salary payments from a known employer
tasks.reasoning: Threshold avoidance, unclear funds and evasiveness together increase suspicion.
tasks.tip: One flag may be innocent; clusters are not.
tasks.mistake: Dismissing clusters of flags is how laundering passes unnoticed.
tasks.recommendation: Write down your reasoning and the evidence behind it so a reviewer can verify your conclusion quickly.

tasks.title: Tipping Off
tasks.prompt: After filing a suspicious activity report, the customer asks why a deposit was delayed. What should you do?
options: Give a neutral, non-committal reply and not disclose the report
Ask them to withdraw the funds
tasks.reasoning: Tipping off may be a criminal offence and compromises investigations.
tasks.tip: Follow the script; escalate questions to compliance.
tasks.mistake: Disclosing a report can obstruct the investigation.
tasks.recommendation: Write down your reasoning and the evidence behind it so a reviewer can verify your conclusion quickly.

tasks.title: SAR Narrative
tasks.prompt: Write a 3-5 sentence SAR narrative for this case. Do not accuse; describe facts and reasons for suspicion.
tasks.modelAnswer: On four consecutive days the customer deposited CHF 9,500 in cash, totalling CHF 38,000, each just below the CHF 10,000 reporting threshold. The customer was unable to explain the source of funds. The director is a close relative of a senior public official, which presents elevated corruption risk. We cannot confirm the origin of the funds and consider the pattern consistent with structuring. Supporting documents: transaction records, KYC file and call notes are attached.
tasks.reasoning: A SAR states who, what, when, how much and why it is suspicious, using facts only.
tasks.mistake: Opinions and accusations weaken the report and create legal risk.
tasks.recommendation: Write down your reasoning and the evidence behind it so a reviewer can verify your conclusion quickly.

caseStudy.title: Case Study: The Alerts Nobody Escalated
caseStudy.background: A bank's monitoring system produced thousands of alerts. Analysts closed repetitive ones as 'false positives' without checking the pattern, and a laundering network moved CHF 4M over two years.
caseStudy.challenges: Alerts were closed individually; no one looked across time.
caseStudy.constraints: Targets focused on closing alerts quickly.
questions: Why does closing alerts quickly create risk?
How should repeat alerts be handled?
caseStudy.solution: Quantis added pattern-based alert grouping and required rationale for each closure.
caseStudy.lessonsLearned: Compliance is about patterns and documented reasoning, not alert counts.

options: Disclosing a report to the customer

quiz.q: In the case study the problem was:
options: Alerts were closed without looking at patterns

prompts: Which red flag would you have escalated first?
